title: Introduction to Incentives
narration_text:
Related: Aligning Incentives and the Academic Paper.

Remember when your grandparents funded World War Two by buying war bonds?
context: The narrator introduces the historical concept of war bonds as a parallel to health funding.

title: A Good Deal
narration_text:
They got roughly three percent returns and a world without Nazis (mostly). Good deal.

You're doing the same thing.
context: Explaining the return on investment for WW2 bonds and drawing a comparison to modern needs.

title: War Bonds for Diseases
narration_text: Except instead of buying bonds to kill Nazis, you're buying bonds to kill diseases. War bonds, but backwards.
context: The narrator frames the new financial instrument as a way to eradicate diseases through investment.

title: The Institutional Core Problem
narration_text:
The Core Problem: Good Ideas Die in Committee.

Here's your species' fun puzzle: you know how to save millions of lives.
context: Identifying the central hurdle: human systems fail to implement known life-saving solutions.

title: The Failure to Act
narration_text:
You can measure exactly how many. You have the money. You don't do it.

Not because your politicians are evil.
context: Clarifying that the failure to save lives isn't due to malice, but systemic design.

title: Political Self-Interest
narration_text:
Because your system is built so that:

Politicians maximize reelection, status, and post-office careers, not "humans continuing to exist".
context: The narrator explains how political incentives are focused on personal career gain rather than global survival.

title: Bureaucratic and Lobbyist Goals
narration_text:
Bureaucracies maximize budget and turf, not "speed of treatments".

Lobbyists maximize client profits, not "global welfare".
context: Listing the misaligned incentives of government departments and corporate lobbyists.

title: Ineffective Awareness
narration_text: You don't fix this with awareness campaigns. You've been "raising awareness" for decades and everyone is still dying,
context: A critique of traditional social advocacy methods that fail to change the underlying system.

title: The White Paper Problem
narration_text: but they're dying aware, so that's nice. You don't fix it with white papers. Politicians use white papers to stabilize wobbly tables.
context: Sarcastic commentary on the lack of impact from academic reports and awareness efforts.

title: Lessons from Wishonia
narration_text:
You fix it by changing WHAT SELF-INTEREST POINTS AT.

On Wishonia, we used something very similar to bootstrap the whole transition
context: The narrator suggests shifting self-interest, citing a historical precedent from their home planet.

title: Evolving Usefulness
narration_text: four thousand, two hundred and ninety-seven years ago. We don't need them anymore (people do useful things because they're useful,
context: Describing the long-term shift on Wishonia toward doing good for its own sake.

title: Historical Skepticism
narration_text: which I realize sounds made up, but you also thought "washing your hands" sounded made up until eighteen forty-seven).
context: Drawing a parallel to how radical health ideas were once dismissed by humans.

title: The Legal Bribe
narration_text:
The point is: you need them now.

This chapter describes how to legally bribe your politicians into doing the right thing.
context: Introducing the concept of using financial incentives to steer political behavior legally.

title: Incentive Alignment Bonds
narration_text: Incentive Alignment Bonds (I.A.B.s): a financial instrument for paying for better governance without technically paying politicians,
context: Defining IABs as a tool for governance reform without legal or ethical violations.

title: The Politics Constraint
narration_text:
giving money to governments, or going to prison.

Your one percent Treaty isn't constrained by physics, biology, or money.
context: Emphasizing that funding and science aren't the bottlenecks; human governance is.

narration_text: It's constrained by POLITICS, which is like being constrained by your dog's opinion on quantum mechanics,
context: A humorous comparison to illustrate the absurdity of political obstacles in the face of science.

title: The Fear of Military Cuts
narration_text:
except your dog can veto legislation.

No politician wants to be the one who "cut the military." Even by one percent.
context: Highlighting the political suicide associated with redirection of defense spending.

title: The Attack Ad Cycle
narration_text: Even if that one percent cures cancer. The attack ads write themselves: "Senator Johnson voted to WEAKEN AMERICA."
context: Visualizing how beneficial reforms are weaponized in political campaigns.

title: A Working, Broken System
narration_text: Your system does exactly what it's incentivized to do. It's not broken. It's working perfectly at the wrong thing.
context: The narrator explains that the current outcome is the natural result of existing incentives.

title: The Proposed Fix
narration_text: The fix: tell every politician on Earth, "Vote for a one percent-style reform and you get better reelection odds
context: Proposing a global offer to politicians to align their career success with health reform.

title: Rewards for Retirement
narration_text: and a Goldman Sachs board seat when you retire." No backroom deals. No suitcases of cash. Just a standing, public rule:
context: Explicitly linking public good acts to prestigious and lucrative post-retirement opportunities.

title: No Morality Required
narration_text: do the objectively good thing, and the world systematically rewards you. Nobody has to become a better person.
context: The narrator stresses that this system works on pragmatism rather than moral evolution.

narration_text:

Same structure as green bonds and catastrophe bonds.
